harms.add: In a Thai cohort, men who reported long spells of heat at work were about twice as likely to report a new kidney diagnosis. In Sri Lanka, heat at work alone does not explain the kidney disease of unknown cause found among farmers.

sources.label: Tawatsupa et al., Journal of Epidemiology, 2012: occupational heat and kidney disease in the Thai Cohort Study
De Silva et al., 2022: occupational heat exposure alone does not explain CKDu in Sri Lanka

harms.add: A review of seven studies across 61 countries links heat built up over months and years with poorer results, hardest on low-income students.

sources.label: Vasilakopoulou et al., PLOS Climate, 2025: cumulative urban heat and learning, a systematic review

harms.add: In rural India, a hot growing season was followed by poorer diets the next year among the households that already ate least, a gap that averages hide (a working paper).

sources.label: Stainier et al., NBER working paper, 2025: hot weather, undernutrition and adaptation in rural India

harms.add: In a national survey of Thai adults, people whose daily life was often disrupted by heat reported poorer wellbeing; a survey like this cannot show which came first.

sources.label: Tawatsupa et al., BMJ Open, 2012: heat stress, health and wellbeing in a national cohort of Thai adults

harms.add: In Dhaka, informal workers described paying for treatment and borrowing during heat; how long such debts last is not yet known.

sources.label: IIED, 2026: health and economic impacts of heat on informal workers in urban Bangladesh

harms.add: Personal sensors worn by women aged 40 to 79 in rural Tamil Nadu sometimes read more than 5 °C apart within the same hour, so area averages can misjudge who is exposed.

sources.label: Deshpande et al., 2023: heat exposure among adult women in rural Tamil Nadu (PMC10785747)

harms.add: A review of 11 studies finds heat linked to poorer sleep among people who work in it.

sources.label: Raja et al., Annals of Occupational and Environmental Medicine, 2026: heat and sleep among heat-exposed workers, a systematic review

links: Without toilets at work, people drink less in the heat, which adds to the strain on the kidneys.
Kidney disease means missed work for patients and for the family members who care for them.
When heat cuts harvests and farm income, children's test results fall.
A poor harvest leaves the households that already eat least eating less the following year.
Care work crowds out paid work, especially for women who work from home.

watch.text: In 16 Ahmedabad homes compared over one week, most roof treatments lowered daytime indoor heat, but one coating left rooms hotter than untreated roofs. Designs differ, and night-time effects were not measured.

sources.label: Vellingiri et al., 2020: cool roofs and indoor temperatures in Ahmedabad's informal settlements (PMC7227734)

atRisk.fact: Personal sensors worn by women aged 40 to 79 in rural Tamil Nadu sometimes read more than 5 °C apart within the same hour, possibly from cooking on solid fuels.

Among 272 people with chronic kidney disease at a Sri Lankan hospital in 2019, the median monthly cost of haemodialysis care was LKR 38,540, including income lost by patients and carers. The study did not look at heat.

source.label: Rathnayake et al., BMC Health Services Research, 2026

questions.q: Which repeated heat exposures lead to kidney harm that lasts beyond the hot season?
questions.have: Single tests in Tamil Nadu and self-reports in Thailand raise the concern; persistent harm and other causes are hard to separate, and heat alone does not explain Sri Lanka's kidney disease of unknown cause.
questions.could: Follow workers before, during and after the hot season, with personal exposure, drinking and repeat kidney tests at least three months apart.
questions.scale: Illustrative: a few hundred workers over two hot seasons

questions.q: When does borrowing for treatment and lost income in a heatwave leave debt outstanding after the season?
questions.have: Worker accounts from Dhaka describe borrowing; repayment over time is rarely tracked.
questions.could: Keep monthly household accounts alongside illness records and local heat, with cooler months for comparison.
questions.scale: Illustrative: a few hundred households over two years

questions.q: Does a cooler night help people recover for the next day's work without adding costs they cannot afford?
questions.have: Studies link heat with poorer sleep, and small roof comparisons measured daytime heat; the two have not been tested together in the region.
questions.could: Try night cooling in a crossover design, measuring bedroom heat, sleep, next-day function and spending.
questions.scale: Illustrative: a few hundred workers over six weeks

questions.q: How does heat shift unpaid care, housework and paid work done at home?
questions.have: Surveys show heat getting in the way of housework and care competing with paid work, but little time accounting.
questions.could: Collect time diaries from several household members in hot and cooler weeks, with indoor heat.

questions.q: Does repeated heat at home affect babies' growth, once diet and infections are taken into account?
questions.have: A study in Bangladesh was found but its full text could not be checked, so no effect is shown on the map.
questions.could: Follow families from pregnancy into infancy with home heat, feeding, infections and measured growth.
questions.scale: Illustrative: a few hundred families over two years

evidence.title: Impacts of heat on sleep quality among heat-exposed workers: a systematic review
evidence.venue: Annals of Occupational and Environmental Medicine

review.finding: Across 11 studies, heat was linked to poorer sleep among people who work in it. This supports the heat and sleep part of the cycle; few studies follow heat built up over a season.
review.limit: Mostly cross-sectional studies with different measures, so the results were not pooled.
